group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old man was evaluated this afternoon in the vascular surgery optimization suite three days before a scheduled elective transperitoneal repair of a 5.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm that was discovered incidentally on surveillance ultrasound for chronic kidney disease; the operating team anticipates a midline incision from xiphoid to pubis, proximal aortic clamping below the renal arteries, interposition of a Dacron tube graft, cross-clamp time of roughly 40 minutes, total operative duration approaching four hours, blood loss in the 600–800 mL range, and postoperative admission to the surgical intensive-care unit for overnight ventilatory weaning and hemodynamic monitoring. He drove himself to the hospital, walked the length of the main corridor at an unhurried pace without shortness of breath, and stated that at home he mows his quarter-acre lawn with a self-propelled mower and climbs a full flight of stairs to the bedroom while conversing comfortably on the phone. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, exertional chest tightness, palpitations, or syncope, and he has never required loop diuretics or echocardiography for ventricular dysfunction. Past medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed twenty years ago; oral agents sufficed until six years ago when fasting plasma glucose drifted above 180 mg/dL, prompting initiation of basal insulin glargine. Three years ago prandial insulin lispro was added when hemoglobin A1c exceeded 8.5 %. He currently injects 34 units of glargine subcutaneously each night and counts carbohydrates at meals using a 1-unit-per-10-gram ratio for lispro with a correction factor of 1 unit for every 25 mg/dL above a target of 130 mg/dL; glucometer downloads reviewed today show pre-breakfast values ranging from 112 to 168 mg/dL over the past month with no documented hypoglycemia. Five years earlier he suddenly developed right-sided facial droop and expressive aphasia while eating lunch; neuroimaging demonstrated a left frontal cortical infarct without large-vessel occlusion, intravenous alteplase was administered within the treatment window, and deficits resolved completely after three weeks of outpatient speech therapy. He has experienced no recurrent focal neurologic events, and duplex sonography last year revealed 40 % bilateral internal carotid narrowing that did not warrant intervention. Long-standing hypertension is managed with amlodipine 5 mg every morning and lisinopril 20 mg nightly; home pressures logged by the patient average 124–132/70–76 mm Hg. Hyperlipidemia is treated with atorvastatin 40 mg each evening, and the most recent low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was 78 mg/dL. He quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 30-pack-year exposure, drinks one bottle of light beer with Friday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Prior procedures include laparoscopic appendectomy at age 40 and left inguinal hernia repair at 57, both uneventful. Family history is significant for a father who died of complications of an aortic aneurysm rupture at 72 and a mother who required dialysis for diabetic nephropathy in her late sixties. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, claudication, chronic cough, abdominal pain beyond occasional dull mid-abdominal fullness from the aneurysm, gastrointestinal bleeding, or urinary changes. After five minutes of quiet sitting, vital signs obtained in the right arm showed blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, height 178 cm, weight 91 kg, and body-mass index 28.7 kg/m². He appeared well nourished and in no acute distress. Jugular venous pulsation was not visible at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was localized in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line without displacement or heave. First and second heart sounds were crisp with no gallop, rub, or murmur. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. Abdominal examination revealed a pulsatile, nontender midline mass superior to the umbilicus consistent with the known aneurysm, no bruits, and active bowel sounds. Peripheral pulses were 2 + in radial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis distributions without asymmetry; there was no peripheral edema or skin discoloration. Neurologic screening demonstrated full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Anesthesia airway assessment documented Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor gap 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension. Preoperative laboratory studies drawn one hour before examination revealed hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 248 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.5 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 44 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.9 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 24 mL/min/1.73 m²; simultaneous fasting glucose measured 144 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displayed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, axis 40°, and no ST-segment deviation compared with a tracing from two years ago. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette without pulmonary congestion or pleural effusion. The perioperative plan is to continue antihypertensive and statin therapy on the morning of surgery, reduce the bedtime glargine dose by 20 % the night before, withhold prandial lispro after midnight until point-of-care glucose is checked pre-induction, employ balanced general anesthesia with invasive arterial monitoring and a triple-lumen central venous catheter, guide crystalloid and colloid replacement with stroke-volume variation to avoid both hypovolemia and fluid overload in the setting of marginal renal reserve, administer cell-salvage autotransfusion as needed, place sequential compression devices before induction, and commence subcutaneous unfractionated heparin on the evening of postoperative day 0 for thromboembolism prophylaxis. After all elements of the operative strategy, potential complications including hemorrhage, graft infection, renal deterioration, spinal cord ischemia, respiratory failure, and recurrent neurologic events were discussed, the patient accurately restated fasting and medication instructions and expressed readiness to proceed with definitive aneurysm repair.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns one point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery: planned open transperitoneal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: no documented history → 0.
- Congestive heart failure: no history or clinical evidence → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior ischemic stroke counts despite complete recovery → 1.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses glargine and lispro → 1.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: 2.9 mg/dL → 1.
Sum: 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
Final answer: 4
